With these she mingles her beatings and much beats her unworthy
breast bloody, the sea-blue sisters answer her laments:
as in the Isthmian harbour, not yet a Nereid,
they say Leucothea bewailed, while with panting breast
the cold infant spat back the savage sea against his mother.
But the father Ismenos, residing in his secret cave,
whence the breezes and clouds drink and the rain-bearing bow
is fed and a better year comes into the Tyrian fields,
when the laments from afar, though he himself roars over them, and the new
groans of his daughter he received, lifts his neck rough with moss
and his hair heavy with frost, and the grown pine fell,
loosed from his hand, and the dismissed urn rolls away.
Him, thrusting forth along the banks his crag-like face
of aged mud, the woods and the lesser rivers
marvel at: so great he rises from the swollen gulf,
lifting his foaming crest, and with sounding fall
his breast streaming with rivulets from his sea-blue beard.
One of the Nymphs, meeting him, teaches her father the kindred
groans and the fall of his grandson, and points out the bloody
author and presses his right hand: he stood towering in the deep
river, and shaking with his hand his cheeks and his horns bound
with green sedge, thus turbulent with deep mouth
he begins: 'Is this the honour, ruler of the gods above, for me,
that, so often both host to your deeds and conscious of them —
nor is it fear to recall — I saw the false, impudent
horns upon your brow, now Phoebe forbidden to unyoke her chariot,
the dowered pyres and the deceived thunderbolts,
and reared the chief of your sons? Or is even to them
gratitude cheap? To this river surely the Tirynthian crept,
in this water we quenched blazing Bromius for you.
Behold what slaughters, what funerals I bear in my stream,
continuous with weapons and covered with another heap.
Every ford the chain of war holds, every
wave pants with crime, beneath and above fresh souls
wander and join the twin banks with darkness.
I, that river called upon in sacred howls,
who am said to wash the soft thyrsi and the Bacchic horns
in my pure fount, crammed with slaughters seek narrow
ways into the sea; not so do the impious pools of Strymon
swim with so much blood, not more deeply does foaming Hebrus
redden when Gradivus wars, nor does the nursing
wave warn you, and your own hands, long since forgetful of your parents,
Liber? Or is Eastern Hydaspes better pacified?
But you, who, swollen, rejoice in the spoils and blood
of a guiltless boy, not from this river, victor, will you bear back
mighty Inachus or savage Mycenae,
unless I am mortal and your blood led from the aether.'
So he speaks, gnashing, and of his own accord to the raging waves
gave the signal: cold Cithaeron sends down its mountain
aid and its ancient snows, and bids the winter's
pastures go; the brother Asopos to him as he goes
reconciles his silent strength and supplies streams
from gaping veins. He himself searches the bowels of the hollow earth
and the pools and the torpid lakes and the sluggish marshes
he shakes out, and, lifting his greedy face to the stars,
he drains the dripping mists and dries the air.
And now over his banks he went, taller on either
mound, now Hippomedon, who but now had overcome the mid
river untouched by the waters in shoulders and hands,
marvels that the ford has grown and that he is the lesser,
on this side and on that swollen waves and a spirited
tempest rises like the sea, when it drinks down the Pleiades
or dashes black Orion against the trembling sailors,
not otherwise the Teumesian river tosses Hippomedon
on its sea-like swell, and ever by the left boss
he is lifted, and the swell with its blackening surge overruns his shield,
foaming as it leaps, and the broken wave pours back
and returns with a greater heap; nor content with its liquid mass
it tears the crumbling trees that guard the rotten banks
and the aged beams, and rolls the stones cast up from the bottom,
the fight stands unequal, of the river and the man,
the god indignant; for he neither gives his back nor by any
threats is broken, and meeting the coming waves
he enters and drives apart the streams with his opposed buckler,
his steps stand though the earth flees, and with knee braced
he holds the slippery rocks, and pressing on his knees and clinging
he keeps his footing, undermined by the treacherous slime,
thus even chiding: 'Whence is this, Ismene, suddenly
your wrath? Or from what gulf have you drawn these strengths,
servant of an unwarlike god, and knowing blood only
from the women's dances, when the Bacchic boxwood lows
and the mad mothers stain the triennial feast?'
He had spoken; and the god of his own accord presented himself,
turbulent in cheeks with rain and a cloud of swimming sand,
nor rages in words, but with a lopped oak his breast
thrice, four times he drove, as far as wrath and the god availed,
rising up against the man: at last he bent his footing,
and the covering struck from his hand, and slowly turning
his back he bears it off, the waves press and the river follows
the staggering man, exulting; nor do the Tyrians fail with stones and a hail
of iron from above to assail him, and with the twin
mound repel him; what should he do, besieged by wars and waves?
Now there is for the wretch no flight, nor leave for a great death.

title: Thebais
text:
There stood, jutting from the grassy ledge of the bank,
at the boundary of waters and earth, but friendlier to the waters,
an ash, and had possessed the ford with its huge shadow;
its help — for by what way should he invade the lands? — with hooked
right hand he seized: nor did it bear him as he dragged;
but, overcome by a greater weight than that on which it stood,
it is loosed, and where with its root it enters the pools and with which
it bit the dry ground, sent down from above
it cast itself upon the trembling man and the bank, nor further
allowing the man to pass, it walled it with a bridge of sudden ruin.
Hither the waves come together, and inescapable in mire
and in hollow whirlpools a pit settles and grows;
and now the winding chasm circles the leader's shoulders, now his neck:
here at last conquered to confess the worst
he cries out: 'In a river — for shame! — famed Mars, will you drown
this life, and shall I go beneath the sluggish lakes and pools
like the guard of a flock, intercepted by the unjust
waters of a sudden torrent? Did I so deserve not
to fall by the steel?' At last, moved by his prayers,
Juno approaches the Thunderer: 'How far, famed sower of the gods,
the wretched Inachidae, how far will you press them? Now both Pallas hates
Tydeus, now, the augur snatched, Delphi has fallen silent:
behold my Hippomedon, whose race's origin is Mycenae
and the Argive household gods and, before all, the power of Juno —
am I thus faithful to my own? — shall he go, a prey
to the cruel beasts of the sea? Surely you used to give the swollen ones
and the last rites to the conquered; where, after the battles, the Cecropian
flames, where is the fire of Theseus?' He does not scorn the fair
prayers of his wife, and lightly to the walls of Cadmus turned
his eyes, and at the seen nod the streams subsided.
His bloodless shoulders and pierced breast lie open:
as when a tempest, lifted high by the winds, has settled,
the crags rise and the land sought by the sailors,
and the seas descend from the threatening rocks.
What does it avail to have held the banks? On every side a cloud
of weapons the Phoenician cohort presses, nor is there any cover
for his limbs, and all lies open to death; then the wounds flow,
and the blood that long stood numb beneath the river, in the bare air
is loosed, and relaxes the thin gapings of the veins,
and his steps falter, uncertain from the cold of the waters,
he falls, as on Getic Haemus falls
either by the furies of Boreas or its rotten timber an oak
that mingled its locks with heaven, and looses a vast space of air:
at it, nodding, the grove and the very mountain tremble,
on what ground it shall fall, what woods in order it shall overwhelm.
Yet there is for none the daring to touch his sword or helmet;
scarce do they trust their eyes, and shudder at the huge
funeral, and approach close with arms drawn tight.
At last Hypseus came up and from him, holding the hilt in death,
draws it and loosed the grim face from the helmet;
and he goes through the Aonians, showing on high on his gleaming
point the hung helmet, and exults with a shout:
'Here is fierce Hippomedon, here the dread avenger
of unspeakable Tydeus and the conqueror of the bloody
gulf!' Far off great-souled Capaneus knew him and pressed down
his grief, and a huge weapon on his arm,
balancing, he urges himself: 'Be present, O to me, my right hand, only
you present in wars and an inescapable power,
you I call, you alone, despiser of the gods above, I adore.'
So he speaks, and makes himself master of his own vow,
the trembling fir goes through the shield and the bronze webs
of the corselet, and at last beneath the great breast
catches the soul: he falls with no other crash than a lofty
tower when, shaken deep within by countless blows,
it slips and opens the broken city to the victors,
standing over whom: 'We do not deny the honour
of death,' he says; 'turn your eyes hither, I am the author of your wound;
go glad and much prouder than the other shades!'
Then he snatches the sword and helmet and tears off the shield
of Hypseus; and holding it over lifeless Hippomedon:
'Receive,' he says, 'at once the hostile spoils, great leader, and your own,
the honour will come to your ash and its own order
to your ghost; meanwhile, while we render the just fires,
this avenger Capaneus covers your limbs with this tomb.'
So, doubtful by war's hard turn, mutual to the Greeks
and the Sidonians alike, Mavors wove their wounds:
here fierce Hippomedon, there no less nimble Hypseus
is wept, and the alternate griefs give solaces.

title: Thebais
text:
Meanwhile, her sleep troubled by sad shapes,
the grim mother of the arrow-bearing Tegean youth,
her hair let down everywhere and her soles, by custom, bare,
before day was going to the cold waters of Ladon
to purge the evil dream in the living river,
for through nights stunned by the weight of cares
often she had seen both the spoils, slipped from the shrine she herself
had dedicated, and herself wandering among unknown tombs,
exiled from the groves and put to flight from the company of Dryads,
often that her son's new triumphs had returned from war,
and the arms and the wing-footed horse she knew and the comrades she saw,
never himself; now that the quivers had slipped from his shoulders,
and her own effigies and known images burned.
But chief terrors that night seemed to portend
to the wretched woman, and roused the mother with all her breast.
Through the Arcadian woods there was an oak of happy strength,
which she herself had consecrated to Trivia,
chosen from the crowd of the grove, and by worship had made it
a power: here she was wont to lay up her bow and her wearied weapons,
and to fix her curved arms and the backs of emptied lions
and horns rivalling the huge woods.
Scarce was there room for the branches, so do all the rustic
spoils gird them, and the gleam of iron hinders the green shadow.
This, as by chance she returned from the ridges, wearied by long
hunting, just then fierce, bearing the snatched face
of an Erymanthian bear, she sees, torn by many a wound,
to have laid down its leafage and, its boughs dripping with blood,
to breathe out upon the ground; to her asking, a Nymph said the bloody
Maenads and the enemy Lyaeus had raged.
While she groans and surrounds her breast with vain beating,
her eyes broke off the night, and from her mournful couch
she leaps, and through her eyes seeks the false weeping.
Therefore, when in the river she had thrice purged the horror, her hair plunged,
and added words to console the anxious cares of mothers,
she rushed to the shrine of armed Diana
beneath the Eastern dew, and the known woods in order
and the oak, glad, she sees; then at the goddess's threshold
she stood and with such a voice prays in vain:
'Maiden mighty over the groves, whose not soft standards
and grim warfare, disdaining my sex, I follow
in no Greek fashion — nor have the harsh Colchians by their rite
nor the Amazonian bands worshipped you more — :
if to me there was never a thiasus or the sport of an insolent
night, and, though defiled by a hated couch,
yet I bore neither the rounded thyrsi nor the soft
spinning, but in the gloomy haunts and after my marriage
thus too a huntress, and unwed I remained in spirit:
nor was it my care to hide my fault beneath secret caves,
but I showed my offspring and laid him trembling
before your feet, confessing; nor was he degenerate
from my blood, and at once he crept upon my bows,
the boy demanded weapons with tears and his first voice:
him to me — what do the troubled nights and the dream threaten? —
him, I pray, who now to the battles with a bold vow,
alas trusting too much in you, has gone, grant me to see the war's
victor, or, if I ask too much, grant me only to see him!
Here let him sweat and bear your arms, press down the dire signs
of evils; why in our woods, woodland Delia,
do the enemy Maenads and the Theban powers reign?
Ah me! why deep — and may I be an augur empty of the future! —
why do I interpret the oak with a deep and great omen?
But if sleep sends true presages to the wretched,
by your mother's toils, gentle Dictynna,
and your brother's glory, drive with all your arrows
this unhappy womb; let him hear first the funeral
of his wretched mother!' She said, and, dissolved in weeping,
she sees the stone of snowy Diana too has grown wet.

title: Thebais
text:
The fierce goddess leaves her, still on the sacred threshold
laid out and sweeping the cold altars with her hair,
and over leafy Maenalus, amid the stars,
she rises in a leap and aims her step to the walls of Cadmus,
where the inner path of heaven gleams
for the gods alone, and, lofty, she sees all the lands beside her.
And now she held nearly the middle of her journey, past the leafy
neck of Parnassus, when she sees her brother in a gleaming cloud
with no wonted look: he was returning from the Echionian
arms, mournful, mourning the funeral of the drowned
augur. The region of heaven reddened with the star's mingling,
and at the sacred meeting the radiance blazed alike on both sides,
and their bows met and their quivers answered.
He first: 'I know, sister, the Labdacian cohorts
and the too-brave Arcadian who has dared the battles you seek.
A faithful mother asks: would that the fates granted
to indulge her praying! Behold, I myself — for shame! — saw, helpless,
the arms of my worshipper and the sacred foliage go down to empty
Tartarus, and his face turned upon me as it descended;
nor did I hold the chariot and force back the broken earth,
savage I and undeserving of worship. You behold the mourning
caverns, sister, and the silent homes: this alone I repay
as gifts to my pious comrade; nor do you stir doomed
aids, and go on with your mournful labours in vain.
The end is near for the youth, this fate is not changeable,
nor do your brother's oracles deceive you about doubtful things.'
'But the last honour at least,' confused in turn
the maiden replies, 'and one may seek solaces for a true
death, nor shall he escape punishment, whoever has stained his unspeakable
right hand, impious, with the blood of a guiltless boy,
and let it be right to rage with our arrows.'
So having spoken she moves her steps, and to her brother more sparingly
offered her lips to be touched, and sought Thebes in hostility.
But the battle, the kings snatched away from both sides, grows fiercer,
and vengeance rouses alternate frenzies.
On this side the squadrons of Hypseus and the host desolate
of their master, but on this the bereaved cohort roars more heavily
for Hippomedon taken away; struggling they offer their bodies to the steel,
the same ardour in the rabid to drink foreign blood
and to have poured out their own, nor do they change their tracks:
the line stands fixed in a wedge, and to the bloody foe
they give their lives and deny their backs: when, slipped through the air,
swift Latonia stood on the summit of the Dircaean
mountain; the hills know her, and the wood
trembles at the known goddess, where once, thrust forth with savage arrows,
she had consumed fertile Niobe with her wearied bow.
Him, proud amid the lines, the slaughter now begun,
ignorant of arms and then enduring the first reins,
a hunter's horse bore along, which a dappled
tigress girds and beats his shoulders with gilded claws,
his neck sits in knots, and the chastised liberty
of his mane, and the known crescents of the grove
upon his breast's front toss in snow-white tooth.
He himself, his mantle twice steeped in Oebalian purple
and his tunics bright with gold — this one work
his mother had spun — gathered at the flanks with a thin band,
had let down his shield on the left shoulder of his steed,
heavy with too great a sword: the golden buckle with rounded
bite delights him, the girdle hanging round his rough sides,
and to hear the sound of the scabbard and the trembling murmur
of the quiver and the chains sent from his cone-crest down his back;
sometimes, glad, to toss his plumed crest
and the jewelled radiance of his helmet, but where the battle
heats the panting headpiece, his crown loosed, bare
he rises forth: then sweet his hair, and trembling with the rays
sweet his looks gleam, and his cheeks, which he himself grieves to delay,
not yet changed with the rosy down,
nor does the praise of his beauty please him, and with stern
threats he much roughens his face, but the comely wrath keeps
the honour of his brow. Of its own accord the Theban youth gives ground,
mindful of their own sons, and turn back their aimed weapons,
but he presses and hurls savage spears at those who pity,
and him, warring through the Teumesian ridges, the Sidonian
Nymphs, pleasing with his very sweat and dust,
praise, and with a silent vow draw their sighs.

title: Thebais
text:
To gentle Diana, beholding such things, grief steals deep
into her high heart, and, her cheeks marred with weeping, 'What now,
a faithful goddess, shall I seek for you, as an escape from near
death? Did you of your own accord hasten into these battles, savage
and pitiable boy? Alas, your raw and hasty valour
counselled it, and the glory that urged your spirited death.
Surely, the years now long pressing, the Maenalian
grove was too narrow for you, little one, and through the caves of beasts
your ways were scarce safe without your mother, whose woodland
weapons and bow you, forward one, could not yet fill.
And now she beats at my altars over your huge
jealousy and wearies the deaf doors and thresholds:
you rejoice in the sweet clarions and the howled battles,
happy, and about to die only to your wretched parent.'
Yet, lest in vain she should have been present at the last honour
of the dying, she comes into the midst, hedged with dusky
darkness, and first, having stolen light arrows,
fills the quiver on the bold boy's back with heavenly
weapons, of which none fell without blood;
then she sprinkles his limbs with ambrosial liquid,
sprinkles his horse, lest his body be seen with a pious wound
before death, and mingles sacred songs and conscious
murmurs, which in secret caves she herself by night
teaches the Colchian women and shows the fierce herbs to those who seek.
Then truly, fiery, with bow drawn forth he flies about,
nor rules himself in mind, of country and mother and self
forgetful, and uses the heavenly arms too much:
as a lion, to whom small his Gaetulian mother
herself supplies the bloody food, when first he felt his neck
grow with mane and grimly looked back at his new claws,
disdains to be fed, and at last, pouring forth, free,
loves the open fields and knows not to return to the caves.
Whom, come, do you lay low, wicked boy, with your Parrhasian horn?
The first arrow troubled Tanagraean Coroebus,
sent through a narrow way at the helmet's edge
and the buckler's outer margin; the wave of blood
stands in his throat, and his face reddens with the fire of the sacred venom.
More savagely Eurytion, into whose left eye's orb
the cunning point hid itself with triple barbs.
He, drawing the full arrow with his slipping eye,
went against the author: but what can the strong weapons of the gods
not do? Another wound, doubled with his other eye,
filled out his darkness; yet the wicked one follows the foe,
where he remembers, until, slipping, he fell on the prostrate
Idas: here the wretch amid the funerals of savage war
quivers and prays for death from comrades and from foes.
He adds the Abantiades, Argus marked by his hair,
and Cydon, ill-loved by his wretched sister.
This one's twin temple he ran through with a slanting arrow,
on this side the iron leaped out, on that the swift feather stayed:
blood flowed on both sides, the harsh weapons of death give pardon
to none, not beauty saved Lamus, not the fillet Lygdus,
not his downy years protected Aeolus:
Lamus is driven in the face, Lygdus is wounded in the groin,
pierced by the weapon you groan, Aeolus, for your snowy brow,
you headlong Euboea bore, you fair Thisbe
had sent, this one the green Erythrae you will not receive.
Never is his hand empty, no missile fled without a power,
nor is there rest for his right hand, and to the former's sound
the following arrow joins, who would believe it one bow
or one hand that raged? Now he directs his strokes,
now on the alternate side, doubtful, he changes his attempts,
now he flees those who press and looks back with his bow alone.

title: Thebais
text:
And now, marvelling and indignant, the Labdacids gathered,
and first of the bright blood of Jove,
Amphion, still ignorant what funerals on the fields
that one was dealing: 'How far will you gain a delay of fate,
O boy about to bereave your much-deserving parents?
Nay, even pride and boldness swell in your mind,
while no one deigns your meetings and your lesser fight
worthy of war, and you are left below their wrath;
go, seek Arcadia again, and there mingled with your equals,
while here fierce Mavors rages in true dust,
play battles at home: but if the mournful fame of a tomb
moves you, we will give you to death, to die by men!'
For long against him the grim son of Atalanta burns
with heavier goads — nor yet had that one ceased — and begins:
'Late even against Thebes, whose army this is, I bring
my arms; who then is so much a boy as to refuse to war
with such men? You see the stock of Arcadia and the fierce seed
of a race, not Theban: not under the silent night
did a Thyiad mother, servant to Echionian Lyaeus,
bring me forth; never have we put on the misshapen mitres
on our heads and shaken the base spear in our hand,
at once I learned to creep across the icebound rivers
and to enter the dread homes of great beasts
and — why should I say more? — the steel and the bow always
my mother holds, your fathers strike the hollow drums.'
Amphion did not bear it, and at his face and at the mouth
of the speaker whirls a huge weapon; but, troubled by the dire
gleam of the iron, his steed twisted itself and its master
to the side and turned aside the greedy spear;
the keener for this Amphion sought the youth with drawn point,
when Latonia in the midst of the field cast
herself and stood before his eyes, meeting all his face.
There clung to the youth, bound by a chaste love,
Maenalian Dorceus, to whom his mother had entrusted the wars
and her own fear and the bold years of the boy.
Then, dissembled in his face, the goddess declares:
'Thus far enough to have harried the Ogygian bands,
Parthenopaeus, enough; now spare your wretched parent,
spare the gods, whoever favour you.' Nor terrified he:
'Let me — I will ask no more — most faithful Dorceus,
lay this man low on the ground, who bears weapons rivalling my weapons
and like attire, and tosses his sounding reins.
His reins I will rule, his attire you shall hang on the lofty
threshold of Trivia, his mother I will present with the captive quivers.'
Latonia heard, and laughed with weeping mingled.
This had seen, for long now in a remote part of heaven,
Venus, embracing Gradivus, and while, anxious, she recalls
Thebes and Cadmus to the man and the grandsons of dear
Harmonia, she stirs the grief pressed beneath her silent heart
in season: 'Do you not see this insolent one, Gradivus,
in her virginity bearing herself in the midst of the gatherings
of men? And how she tempers the bold lines and the Martial
standards? Behold, she even gives and offers to be slain
so many men of our race, to her is valour entrusted,
to her frenzy? It remains for you to shoot the rustic does.'
Roused by the just complaints, into arms leaped down
the War-mighty one, to whom alone, as he rushes through the wandering void,
Wrath is companion, the rest of the Furies sweat at the wars,
nor delay, when, standing by, with harsh warning
he chides the mournful daughter of Leto: 'These battles the father
of the gods does not give you; unless at once, shameless one, you desert
the arm-bearing field, you shall know that not even Pallas is equal to this hand.'
What should she do against him? On this side the Martial spear-point presses,
on this your mother's full distaff, little one, on this the face
of stern Jove: she departs, after these things conquered by shame alone.

title: Thebais
text:
But the father Mavors looks round at the Ogygian wings
and stirs dread Dryas, whose blood's author
was turbulent Orion, and to hate the comrades of Diana
(thence he rages) is his inheritance; this one with the sword seizes
the troubled Arcadians and disarms their leader; in a long column falls
the people of Cyllene and the dweller of shady Tegea,
and the Aepytian leaders and the Telphusian phalanxes,
but he trusts to lay low the youth himself even with wearied hand,
nor saves his strength: for now, weary, here and there
he was changing the squadrons; a thousand presages of a funeral
press, and the clouds of black death go before,
and now the wretch saw his comrades few and the true
Dorceus, now he felt his strength slip away little by little,
felt too his quivers drained on his lighter shoulder;
now less and less he bears his arms, and seems a boy
even to himself, when, dread, with the grim light of his shield
Dryas blazed up against him: a sudden trembling twisted the face
and the bowels of the Arcadian; and as the white swan,
when above it it has looked back at the bearer of the fierce thunderbolt,
longs for the bank of Strymon to gape
and draws its trembling wings into its breast:
so on the youth, the mass of savage Dryas seen,
now no wrath comes, but the horror of death's herald,
yet his arms, the gods and Trivia prayed in vain,
he labours, pale, and gets ready his deaf bow,
and now he presses with weapons and, slantwise into either arm,
touches the horns with his point and his breast with the string,
when the spear of the Aonian leader, sped with a great whirl,
is borne against him, and cuts the slanting bonds of the sounding
string: the strokes perish, and with hands relaxed
the vain darts fell from the upturned bow.
Then the wretch, troubled, let go both reins and arms,
unable to bear the wound, which had entered the cover of his right
shoulder and the easy skin: a second spear-point comes up
and stops the flight of his steed, its hamstring cut,
then Dryas himself falls — a wonder — never of his wound
aware: one day the author of the weapon and the cause will appear.
But the boy, laid in his comrades' arms, to a remote part of the field
is borne — alas, simple age! — and dying he wept
for the horse that lay there; his face fell, his helmet loosed,
and a sick grace breathes out through his trembling looks,
and his neck, shaken thrice and four times by his seized hair,
refuses to stand, and — a thing pitiable even to Thebes —
the purple blood went from his snowy breast,
at last with broken sobbing he says these words:
'I am slipping; go, Dorceus, console my wretched parent.
She indeed, if cares bear true presages,
has seen the sad horror either in sleep or by an omen,
yet you, by pious art keep the trembler in suspense and long
deceive her; nor come suddenly, nor while she holds arms,
and at last, when now you are forced to confess,
say: I have deserved it, mother; unwilling, take your punishment;
a boy, I snatched arms, nor with you holding me back was I still,
nor at last, with you anxious amid the wars, did I spare you.
Live therefore, and rather be wrathful at my spirit,
and now lay aside your fears; in vain from the hill of Lycaeus
anxious you look out, if any far off through the clouds
either a sound or dust raised from our column:
cold I lie on the bare earth, nor anywhere
are you near, who would hold my face and out-breathing mouth.
This hair at least, bereaved parent,' and to be cut he offered
it with his right hand, 'this hair you will take in place of my whole body,
which in vain, I disdaining, you were wont to comb,
to this you will give the obsequies, and among the rites remember
that none blunt my weapons with untried arms
or drive my beloved dogs in any caves more.
But these arms, unhappy in my first campaigns,
burn, or hang them up as the reproach of ungrateful Diana.'

title: Thebais
text:
10. Damp night, hastened on by the commands of Jove, buried the Sun behind the western gate;
nor in pity for the camp of the Pelasgians
or the wealth of Tyre, but grieving that beyond the lines
so many guiltless nations should be cut down by the sword,
the field lies open, hideous with measureless blood:
there they leave their arms and the horses they once rode in pride,
and corpses robbed of pyres and limbs cast aside.
Then a dishonoured company, their standards torn, set apart
their stricken ranks; and the gates, too narrow for the throng
that marched out armed, took back the returning few in their width.
The grief on either side was equal; yet to Thebes there came a comfort,
the four wandering troops of the Danaans left without a leader:
as when widowed ships are steered across a swelling sea,
governed only by god and chance and the storms.
Then the Tyrians resolved no longer to guard their own camp,
but rather to watch the enemy's flight, lest perchance,
content to have returned, they should make for Mycenae: the tally gives the signal
to the watches, and the turns are set; the leaders of the covered night,
Meges by lot and Lycus of his own will, and now in ordered rank
they bring their arms, their feast, their fire; the king steadies them as they go:
'Conquerors of the Danaans — for tomorrow's light is not far off,
nor will the darkness that has come between you and the cowards
last forever — lift up your courage, and bear
hearts worthy of the favouring gods. All the glory of Lerna lies low,
and her chief band: Tydeus has gone down to avenging
Tartarus, Death is amazed at the black augur's sudden shade,
Ismenos swells, having snatched the spoils of Hippomedon,
and to count the Arcadian among warlike trophies is a shame.
The reward is in your hands; nowhere now are the lofty heads of the war,
nor the marked crests of the chiefs through the seven columns;
no doubt Adrastus' old age, and his brother's youth that is worse,
and Capaneus, to be feared in his raving arms, are left.
Come then, and ring the besieged with a wakeful flame!
No man need fear the enemy: you are guarding plunder and wealth
that are now your own.' So he fills the savage
sons of Labdacus with his exhortations, and it pleases them to take up again their spent toils:
just as they were — dust and sweat and blood still
mingled on their limbs — they turned their steps; scarcely suffering the talk
that met them, they shook off even the embraces and the right hands
of their own people from their shoulders; then dividing front and rear
and the curves of the flanks, on every side they girdle the rampart
with hostile fires, as when in a great pack
wolves come together toward nightfall, whom in all the fields
hunger, daring everything, has wasted with long-drawn gaping:
already they press the very folds, vain hope twists their jaws,
the trembling bleating and the rich scents from the sheepfolds drive them on;
what is left, they break their claws against the hard doorposts,
and grind their breasts and dry teeth upon the threshold.

title: Thebais
text:
But far off, suppliant on the margin of the Argive temple,
the throng, and the daughters of Pelops, poured out before their fathers' altars,
beg the help and the return of their own
from sceptre-bearing Juno, and they wear away the painted doors
and the cold stone with their faces, and they teach their little sons to bow down.
Their prayers had already buried the day; the night that follows
joins their cares, and the altars keep watch with heaped-up flames.
A robe too they bring as a gift, whose marvellous weaving
no barren hand had turned, nor any hand parted from a husband,
a veil not to be despised, from the baskets of the chaste goddess,
where purple in many fashions blooms abundant
and kindles, mixed with gold.
There the goddess herself, betrothed to the chamber of the mighty Thunderer,
still without wedlock and about to lay aside, in fear, the name of sister,
with downcast gaze sips the kisses of the boy Jove,
simple, not yet offended by her husband's thefts;
with this veil the Argive matrons had then clothed
the holy ivory, and with tears and lament they prayed:
'Look upon the sacrilegious towers of the Cadmean rival,
queen of the starry pole, and scatter the rebel
mound, and against Thebes — you can — hurl another bolt.'
What should she do? She knows the Fates are set against her Greeks,
and Jove turned away; yet she would not have such prayers
and such gifts come to nothing; still, chance set in her path the moment
for great help: she sees from the high heaven the walls
mocked, and the rampart held by a sleepless watch:
she shuddered at the goads of her anger, and her hair, shaken,
disordered the dread diadem: no more fiercely did she burn
when she resented in the empty stars the Thunderer's burden,
his Herculean offspring and his twin nights of love.
So she resolves to give the Aonians, caught in the sweet
charm of sleep, to death, and bids her Iris
gird herself with her accustomed orbits, and entrusts to her
the whole task. The bright goddess obeys the commands and leaves
the pole, and over the earth is suspended on her long arch.

title: Thebais
text:
Above the misty bed of the western night
and the other Ethiopians, where no star can pierce,
there stands a sluggish grove, and beneath it, in the hollow rocks, a deep cave
runs empty into the mountain, where idle Nature has set
the halls of sluggish Sleep and his untroubled home;
shadowy Quiet and slow Oblivion guard the threshold,
and torpid Sloth with a face that never wakes.
Ease in the forecourt, and Silence, mute, with folded wings,
sit and drive the rough winds from the roof,
and forbid the branches to stir, and take the murmur
from the birds; here is no roar of the sea, though all the shores
cry out, nor any crash of heaven; the very river,
fleeing through the deep valleys nearest to the cave,
falls silent among the rocks and crags: round about the dark
herds, all the cattle lie upon the ground, and the new
shoots droop, and the breath of the earth bends down the grass.
A thousand images of the god the burning Mulciber
had carved within: here clings to his side garlanded Pleasure,
here his companion Toil, sinking into rest; in one place is the couch
shared with Bacchus, in another the cushion that belongs to Love, the offspring of Mars;
deeper, in the lofty inner chambers of the dwelling,
he lies even with Death, and that grim image is seen
by no one. These are the shapes; but the god himself, beneath the moist
caverns, lies upon coverlets piled with sleep-bringing flowers;
his garments exhale a vapour, and beneath his sluggish body
the bedding grows warm, and above the couch a black mist breathes out
from his panting mouth; one hand sustains the hair
fallen from his left temple, the other has let slip, forgotten, the horn;
around him stray the countless Dreams with their wandering faces,
true mingled with false, and grim with soothing,
the shadowy host of night, and they cling to the beams and doorposts,
or lie on the ground; faint, where the gleam circles the hall,
is the light and feeble, and the languid lamps that lure on
the first slumbers breathe out from their sinking flames.

title: Thebais
text:
Here from the blue ether the many-coloured maiden
balanced herself down: the woods shine out, the shadowy Tempe
smiled upon the goddess, and the house, struck by her gleaming girdle,
awakes; but he himself, stirred neither by the bright lamp
nor the sound nor the goddess' voice, lies in the same
posture, until the daughter of Thaumas drove all her rays
upon him and sank deep into his idle eyes.
Then thus the tawny mother of the storm-clouds began to speak:
'Gentlest of the gods, Sleep, Juno bids you fasten down
the Sidonian leaders and the people of savage Cadmus,
who now, puffed up by the issue of the war with the Achaeans,
wakeful guard their rampart and refuse your sway.
Grant so great a prayer; rarely is such a power to be had,
to win Jove appeased, with Juno on your right hand.'
She spoke, and rousing his languid breast with her right hand,
lest her words be lost, she warned him again and again;
he, with the same nodding face, assented to the goddess'
commands; heavier now, Iris departs from the dark caverns
and wakes her dimmed brightness with a heavy rain.
He too quickened his winged step and his windy
temples, and filled the cloak that curved with the chill
of the dim sky, and on his silent course through the air
he is borne, and far over the Aonian fields hangs heavy.
His breath unstrings birds and beasts and herds upon the ground,
and deep within, over whatever circle of the world he flies,
the languid seas sink from the cliffs, the clouds hang
fixed, the woods let down their highest tops,
and more stars fell from the loosened sky.
First the plain felt the god draw near in sudden gloom,
and the countless voices and murmurs of the men
lowered their sound; but when on his moist wings
he settled, and a shadow never thicker than pitch
entered the camp, their eyes wander and their necks go slack,
and the words half-uttered are left in the midst of speech,
and soon they let fall their gleaming shields and the cruel
spears from their hands, and weary their faces sink upon their breasts,
and now all is silent: now the horn-hoofed steeds themselves refuse
to stand, and a sudden ash has carried off their very fires.

title: Thebais
text:
But the same drowsiness does not persuade ease upon the anxious
Greeks, and the gentle power of the night-wandering god
keeps his clouds from their neighbouring camp: everywhere they stand in arms,
indignant at the foul night and at the proud watchers,
when lo, as the gods crazed his mind, a sudden horror
comes over Thiodamas, and with dread tumult
bids him unfold the fates, whether it was the daughter of Saturn
or good Apollo that goaded this new companion,
he leaps into their midst, dreadful to see and hear,
unable to bear the god, whom his frail mind, receiving,
cannot hold: the goads spill over, and naked across his face
stands frenzy, and it stretches his trembling cheeks with uncertain blood
and drains them — his gaze strays here and there —
and the garlands mingled in his hair he lashes over his scattered locks,
as the Idaean mother draws her bloodstained Phrygian
from the shrine with her terrors, and forbids him to know his arms
consumed by the iron; he beats the sacred pines against his breast,
and whirls his bloody hair, and exhausts his wounds
in his running: all the field is afraid, and the tree that tends it
is spattered, and the astonished lions raise the car.
They came to the inmost place of council and the dread house
of the standards, where, long sick with great disasters,
moving the last resorts of fortune, Adrastus took counsel in vain.
The hastily summoned chiefs stand round, each as he was nearest
to the slain, and they guard the places left desolate
by the great kings, not glad, and grieving that they have risen to this,
just as when, the helmsman lost, a ship has broken
its course in mid-passage, and to the rudderless tiller's guidance comes
either the guard of the flanks, or he who held the prow
facing the sea: the very vessel is dazed, and slowly the gear
obeys, nor does its safety come to a lesser master.
So the eager augur thus uplifts the trembling Achaeans:

title: Thebais
text:
'Great commands of the gods, leaders, and dread warnings
I bring; these are no words from my own breast:
he sings them, to whom your trust compelled me to be servant
and to take the fillets, with no protest from himself.
A night fruitful in deeds, and fit for a noble stratagem,
is opened by the gods' augury; manhood calls us to the venture,
and Fortune demands our hands; the legion of the Aonians lies
overwhelmed in sleep: now is the time to avenge the deaths
of the kings and that wretched day; seize your arms and break
the delay of the gates: this is to set the flames beneath our comrades,
this is to bury our own. Indeed both this and in the day's warfare,
while our cause was broken and we fell back routed —
I swear it by the tripods and the new fate of my snatched master —
I saw, and the favourable birds applauded around me.
But now my faith is sure: just now, beneath the silent night,
he himself, he, rising again, the earth loosened,
just as he was — only the shade had stained his yoked horses —
Amphiaraus came to me: not the visions of empty rest
nor what I learned in sleep do I speak; "Will you," he said, "endure to let so great a night
be lost, you idle son of Inachus —
give me back these Parnassian garlands, give me back
my gods — degenerate one? Was it I myself that taught
these secrets of heaven and the wandering courses of the stars?
Go, come, avenge us at least with the sword!" he said,
and seemed to drive me toward this threshold with raised
spear and with his whole car.
Therefore come, the gods must be used; not hand to hand
must the enemy be laid low: the war lies still, and the power to rage is ours.
Will there be any who would not be loath to lift themselves
to mighty fame, while the fates permit? Look, again the birds
of the kindly night; I follow, and though the columns of comrades hang back,
I go alone! And see, he comes himself and shakes the reins.'

title: Thebais
text:
Crying out such things he disturbed the night, and the chiefs
went, kindled, no otherwise than if the same god were in all
their hearts: they burn to go with him and to share his fortunes;
thirty in number, the strength of the squadrons, by his order
he himself chooses; around, the rest of the youth murmur, indignant,
asking why they should stay in camp and keep cowardly
ease: some cry out their high birth, some the deeds of their kin,
some their own, and others demand the lot, on every side they demand the lot,
Adrastus rejoices in adversity and his spirit rises.
So on Pholoe's summit the breeder of swift horses,
when the springtime's brood has renewed his teeming herd,
rejoices, seeing some strain up the steep of the mountain,
some swim the fords, others contend with their parents;
then in his quiet heart he turns over which is fit to bear
the gentle yoke when broken, which has a good back, which is born
for arms and the trumpet, which is the better to rise to the Elean palms:
such was the long-lived leader of the Achaean troop.
Nor does he fail his undertakings: 'Whence this so late and sudden
favour of the gods? What powers have you returned, broken, to Argos?
Is there yet unhappy valour here? And a blood surviving
its race, and do the seeds of spirit endure in our misery?
I praise you indeed, noble youths, and I enjoy this fair
mutiny of my own; but we are preparing a deception and a hidden
battle, movements to be concealed: a crowd is never fit
for secret guile. Keep your courage, look, the avenging day
comes against the enemy; then arms openly, then we shall all go.'
At these words at last the youths' valour, curbed, grew quiet:
no otherwise than if father Aeolus, his cave stirred,
should again with the imperious rock press shut the gate
and bar every way, when now the winds were hoping for the seas.

title: Thebais
text:
Besides, the seer joins to himself Hercules' Agylleus
and Actor: this one apt to persuade, this one boasts in strength
that he has not yielded to his father; three sets of ten comrades in rank,
a column dreadful to the Aonians and to those who stand against them,
he himself, going to the new stealth of a Mavortian war,
lays aside the worshipped, the Phoebean leaves, the insignia of his brow,
and entrusts to the old leader's bosom the honour
of his forehead, and takes on the breastplate and helmet
offered by Polynices' welcome gift; fierce Capaneus weighs
Actor down with a great sword, while he himself, deigning not against the foe
to go by guile or to follow the gods, Agylleus exchanges
the arms of savage Nomius: for what would the bow and the Herculean
arrows have profited in war among the deceiving shadows?
Then through the broken battlements from the rampart of the camp,
lest the heavy groan of the brazen gate cry out,
they hurl themselves in a leap; nor long, and at once a vast
plunder lies on the ground, as if already lifeless and finished off
by many a sword. 'Go, my comrades, wherever the pleasure
of unexhausted slaughter draws you, and with the gods favouring, I pray,
do your full part!' the priest now urges with a clear voice,
'Do you see the cohorts laid out in shameful rotting?
For shame! Did these dare to besiege the Argive gates,
these to guard their men?' So he spoke, and drew his lightning
sword, and with swift hand passed through the dying
ranks; who could count the slaughters, or mark by name
the lifeless throng? He comes on with no order
and leaves the backs and breasts and the murmurs shut within helmets,
and mingles the wandering shades in blood:
this one carelessly stretched on his bedding, this one with steps
slow and slack stumbling against his shield and ill-holding his weapons,
these lying in the midst of their gatherings among wine and arms,
others leaning on their shields, as each, bound fast,
unhappy sleep upon the ground and the last cloud
had overwhelmed him. Nor is the divine power absent: armed Juno,
shaking in her outstretched right hand a moon-lamp,
opens the way and steadies his spirit and shows him the bodies,
he feels the goddess near, but Thiodamas in silence
hides his joy; now his hand is slow, now his iron weary,
and his anger dimmed with too much success.
Not otherwise the Caspian tigress, amid the slaughter of great
bullocks, when her rage, appeased by measureless blood,
has wearied her jaws, and, foul with thick gore,
has blurred her stripes, looks at her deeds and grieves
that her hunger has failed: so the augur, conquered,
strays among the Aonian slaughters; now let him wish for a hundred arms
and a hundred hands for war; now it wearies him to empty
out his idle threats, and he would rather the enemy rose against him.

title: Thebais
text:
Elsewhere the offspring of great Hercules lays waste the sluggish
Sidonians, and Actor elsewhere; its own crowd meets each man
along a bloody path: the grass stands in pools, blackening with gore,
the tents drip with rivers of blood;
the ground steams, and the breath of sleep and of death together
rolls forth; not one of those who lie there lifted his face
or his eyes: with such a shade the winged god broods
over the wretches, and only looses their dying gazes.
Ialmenus, sleepless, had drawn out with lyre and play the last
stars, never to see another dawn,
singing a Sidonian paean; his languid neck,
as the god forces it, lay leftward, and across his lyre
his throat was folded back: through his breast Agylleus
drives the iron, and strikes the hand fitted to the hollow shell,
and the fingers trembling among their own strings.
The dreadful liquor overturns the tables: on every side
flow waters mingled with blood, and Bacchus into the deep
bowls and cups returns; fierce Actor seizes
Thamyris entangled with his brother, Tagus drains Echetlus,
the garlanded man, from behind; Danaus cuts off the head of Hebrus:
unknowing, alas, he is snatched by the fates, and his life flees
cheerful to the shades, having gained the agonies of a fierce death.
Stretched on the cold ground beneath the faithful yokes and wheels,
Calpetus, with his breath, was frightening the Aonian horses
as they grazed on his native turf: his soaking mouth overflows,
and the sleep kindled by wine seethes; lo, the Inachian seer
pierces the throat of the man as he lies, and a vast gush of gore
drove out the wine, and a broken murmur perished in the blood.
That rest was perhaps prophetic for him, and weighed down he saw
in his sleep black Thebes and Thiodamas.
The fourth watch of the sleep-bringing night remained,
when the clouds were empty and not all the stars had their honour,
and Bootes, with his greater wain, fled away from his blast,
and now the very work failed, when provident Actor
calls Thiodamas: 'Enough of this unlooked-for joy
for the Pelasgians: hardly any, I think, of so great a host
have escaped this savage death, save those whom their misshapen life
hides among the deep blood, degenerate ones; set a limit
to success: even dread Thebes has her own divine powers.
Perhaps the gods who favoured us a moment ago withdraw.'
He obeyed, and lifting his dripping palms to the stars:
'Phoebus, the spoils, the rewards of the night you showed,
not yet washed in water — for to you I made this sacrifice —
I, a savage soldier of the tripods and faithful priest,
deliver them, if I have not disgraced your commands and have borne the god
that pressed me; come often, often deign to burst into this mind.
Now to you a raw honour, the maimed arms and the blood of men:
but if ever, Paean, you grant me my native home and the longed-for
temples, Lycian one, so many rich gifts upon your consecrated
doorposts and as many bulls, mindful of my vow, exact.'
He had spoken, and called his comrades back from their glad slaughter.

title: Thebais
text:
Among these had come, by fate, Calydonian Hopleus
and Maenalian Dymas, both beloved of kings,
both companions of kings, who after their deaths, grieving,
chafe at their own life. First Hopleus rouses the Arcadian:
'Have you no care for the shade of your slain king,
illustrious Dymas — whom perhaps even now the birds
and the Theban dogs may hold? What then will you carry back to your country,
Arcadians? Look, against your return comes a stern mother.
Where is the funeral? But in my breast forever Tydeus
rages, robbed of a tomb, though more patient in his limbs,
and not so lamentable for his years cut short,
yet it is my pleasure to go and search the field at random,
in savage fashion, or to burst into the midst of Thebes.'
Dymas takes up his words: 'By these wandering stars I swear,
by the straying shades of my leader, which are to me as a god's power,
the same purpose is in me, wretched as I am; long has my mind,
humble in grief, looked round for a companion, but now I will go first' — and the way
he begins, and turning to the sky with a sorrowful face
he thus speaks: 'Cynthia, ruler of the secret night,
if they say your power varies with threefold shapes
and that you descend into the woods with another face,
that companion lately, the famous nursling of the groves,
that boy of yours, Diana — now at least look back —
is sought,' he says; the goddess kindles with her downturned horns the kindly
star, and bringing her car near showed the corpses.
The plains appear, and Thebes, and high Cithaeron:
so when with thunder evil Jupiter shatters the nocturnal
air, the clouds spring apart and in the clear flash
the stars lie open, and a sudden world is shown to the eyes.
Hopleus too received the rays, and, struck by the same,
sees Tydeus by that light; from afar through the shadows they give
each other signs, rejoicing, and each one, the dear weight,
as if of men restored to life and sent back from cruel death,
lifts upon their bowed necks; nor did they dare for words,
nor to weep long: near at hand the savage day and the judging
sunrise threaten; they go silent through the mournful stillness
with great strides, and grieve that the spent shadows pale.

title: Thebais
text:
The fates are jealous of the dutiful, and chance is a rare
companion of great enterprises; already they see the camp and draw near in spirit,
and the burden grows lighter, when a shadow of sudden dust
and a sound behind them: at his leader's bidding Amphion was driving
the keen horsemen, set to scout the night and the watched
camp, and first through the trackless plain
far off — not yet had the light loosed all the shadows —
he sees something doubtful to the sight, set ablaze, in motion,
and bodies moving; then, the trick discovered, at once
he cries out: 'Halt your step, whoever you are! But that they are enemies
is plain': the wretched men go on, fearing to lead the way and afraid
not for themselves; then he threatens death to the trembling pair and hurls
his spear, and lifts his vain strokes high from afar,
making his hand seem to stray; it stood before the eyes
of Dymas, who by chance was first and checked his step.
But the great-souled Aepytus did not care to waste
his cast, and with fixed weapon pierces Hopleus through the back
and grazed even the shoulders of Tydeus as he hung,
Hopleus sinks, not yet forgetful of his noble leader,
and dies still holding him — happy, if he does not know
the body is taken from him — and so descends to the savage shades.
Dymas, turned about, had seen this and feels the columns
joined behind him, doubtful whether to meet the pressing foe
with prayers or with arms; his anger gave him arms, his fortune to pray,
not to dare, commanded him: confidence in neither course;
his anger put off his prayers; he sets the pitiable body
before his feet, and the heavy tiger-skin which by chance
he wore upon his back, he twists onto his left arm and stands in the way,
thrusting out his drawn sword against them, and turned
to every weapon, ready for slaughter and for death close beside:
as a lioness, whom in her savage lair, having whelped, the hunting
Numidians have surprised, stands erect over her young
with a mind made up and yet uncertain, grinding her teeth grim and pitiable;
she indeed could scatter their bands and break their weapons
with her bite, but love of her offspring conquers her cruel
breast, and amid her wrath she looks round at her cubs.
And now the man's left hand is wrenched away, though Amphion
forbade his men to rage, and the boy is dragged
by the hair, his face turned upward, and then at last, a late suppliant,
lowering his sword, he begs: 'More gently, I pray,
lead him, by the cradle of the lightning-born Bacchus,
by Ino's flight and the years of your own Palaemon!
If any of you has at home the joys of children, if any here
is a father, grant the boy a draught of scant dust
and a small torch! He asks, lo, he himself asks, with silent
face: I would rather glut the unspeakable birds,
yield me to the beasts; it was I who forced the daring of war.'
'Nay,' says Amphion, 'if so great a longing is yours
to bury the king, tell the Pelasgians what mind the timid have for war,
what the broken and bloodless are preparing; bring all out quickly,
and depart, granted your life and your leader's tomb.'
The Arcadian shuddered, and at once filled his heart
to the hilt: 'Was this lacking,' he says, 'to crown my disasters,
that I, a traitor, should disgrace afflicted Argos?
We buy nothing at such a price, nor would he himself wish to be burned so.'
So he spoke, and the breast, torn open with a great wound,
he flung upon the boy, and rolling out his last murmurs:
'Yet meanwhile possess this tomb with me.'
So both, in the longed-for embrace of their kings,
a pair alike in spirit, the Aetolian and the renowned Arcadian,
breathe out their noble souls and take their fill of death.
You too, made sacred, though my songs rise
from a lesser lyre, mindful of you, shall outlast the years.
Perhaps even Euryalus will not scorn you as companion
shades, and the glory of Phrygian Nisus will admit you.

title: Thebais
text:
But fierce Amphion sends men exulting to carry the deeds back to the king
and tell of the stratagem and give back the captive bodies;
he himself presses on to exult over the shut-in Pelasgians
and to show the severed faces of their comrades.
Meanwhile from the height of the walls the Greeks
see Thiodamas returning, and no longer hide their bursting
joy, as they mark the bared swords and the arms red
with fresh slaughter; a new clamour leaps to the great
sky, and from the top of the rampart the columns hang, eager
each to recognize his own. So a flock of new fledglings,
when it has spied its mother far off returning in the air,
longs to go to meet her, and from the edge of its high nest
juts out, gaping, and would now, now fall, did not the mother
with her whole breast bar them, open-winged, and chide them with her loving wings.
And while they count the secret work and the gains of silent
warfare, and fill their own with glad embraces,
and ask for Hopleus and lament the slow Dymas:
lo, hard by, the swift leader of the Dircaean squadron
had come, Amphion; not for long rejoicing in fresh slaughter
he sees the earth seething with countless bands
and a whole people perishing in a single ruin,
that trembling which a touch of heaven's drawn lamp brings;
here he transfixed the young man, and under a single horror together
his voice, his sight, his blood fail, and as he begins his groan
his very horse turns him away; the squadron flees, their dust
whirled back, not yet were they nearing the barriers of Thebes,
and already the Argive cohort, trusting in their nocturnal triumph,
leaps into the fields; over the arms and the limbs of the fallen
and the foul heap on the soil and the half-living blood
the horn-hoofed steeds and the men themselves rush: the heavy hoof
grinds the limbs, a bloody rain washes and clogs the axles.
Sweet it is to the men to go this way, as if they trampled the proud
Sidonian roofs and Thebes itself in blood.
Capaneus exhorts them: 'Long enough, Pelasgians, has valour
lain hidden and concealed: now, now it is glorious for me to conquer
with the day as witness; come with me openly, in clamour and dust,
youths, in the open: I too have foretelling
omens in my right hand and the dread fury of a drawn sword.'
So he speaks; eager Adrastus kindles the blazing men,
and the Argive son-in-law, and the augur follows now more grim,
and now they press the walls — and still Amphion tells of fresh deaths —
and they would at once have entered the wretched city,
had not Megareus swiftly cried from the high watchtower:
'Close, watchman, the enemy come, close the gates on every side!'

title: Thebais
text:
There is a case where excessive fear gives strength: more swiftly every
gate comes together; while Echion alone, more slowly, closes
the Ogygian gate, the Spartan youth, bold in spirit,
burst in, and the slain fall on the first threshold,
Panopeus, dweller of Taygetus, and the stiff swimmer
Oebalus of Eurotas; and you, watched in all the wrestling-grounds
and lately fortunate in the Nemean dust,
Alcidamas, whom Tyndareus himself had bound
with your first gloves, dying you look back to the vault
of your shining master: equally with the turning of his star the god sets;
you the Oebalian grove, you the slippery bank of the Laconian
maiden and the stream sung of by the false swan
shall weep; you the Amyclaean nymphs of Trivia shall mourn,
and the mother who schooled you in the laws and the brave precepts
of war shall complain that you learned too well.
Such is Mars raging on the Echionian threshold.
At last Acron, straining with his shoulders, and Ialmenides,
bent forward with his whole breast, turned the oaken bulk
of the bronze-bound gate: with as great a groaning neck together
the bullocks break through the long-unploughed Pangaean fields.
The cost of the work matched its gain, for, the enemy shut in,
they shut out their own; within the walls the Greek
Ormenus falls, and as Amyntor stretches forth his arms
and pours out his prayers, deep in his loosened neck
his words and face fall to the ground, and the torque, fair
on his neck, fell through the wound onto the hostile sands.
Meanwhile the rampart is loosed, and the first delays refuse
to stand; now the bands of footmen have joined themselves
to the walls: but to cross the wide ditches at a leap
is a horror to the horses, the trembling beasts hold back and, dreading
the chasm, marvel that it should be crossed; now an onset goes
from the very edge, now of themselves they shrink against the rein.
These tear up the defences fixed in the soil, while those
lessen the barriers of the gates and sweat to heave back
the iron bars, and with beams and ringing bronze
drive the stones from their place; some exult that the torches flung
at the rooftops have caught, some assail the foundations
and search the hollow towers with a blind tortoise-roof.
But the Tyrians, their one safety, crown every head
of the walls, and dark stakes and javelins bright with iron
and bullets that will burn through the empty sky
and stones torn from their very walls they hurl
against the foe: the battlements overflow with a savage storm,
and the armed windows vomit hissing weapons,
just as above Malea or high Ceraunia
the clouds settle, lingering, and are set upon the dark
hills, and sudden squalls leap upon the sails:
so the Argive army is overwhelmed by Agenor's arms;
the dread rain bends neither the faces nor the breasts of the men,
they hold their gazes straight upon the walls,
heedless of death and seeing only their own weapons.
Antheus, sweeping along the walls in his scythed car,
the heavy onset of an Ogygian spear struck down from above;
the reins were shaken from his hand, and rolled back onto his shoulders,
his half-living limbs hang, held by his greaves;
a marvel to see, the crime of war: the arms are dragged,
the smoking wheels furrow the earth, and a third furrow
the spear ploughs; the wandering neck follows in a long trail of dust,
and the broad track of his upturned hair lies open.

title: Thebais
text:
But the trumpet beats the city with mournful blasts
and breaks through the barred doors with its bitter sound,
they have divided the approaches, and on every threshold the savage
standard-bearer, before all others, carrying his own loss and joy,
a dread sight within; scarcely could Mars himself rejoice
to see it; the city, maddened with insane horrors,
they tear apart with various discord, Grief and Frenzy
and Panic and Flight wrapped in blind darkness;
you would think the war had entered: the citadels seethe with running to and fro,
the streets are confounded with clamour, on every side they see
iron and fire in their minds, in their minds they have taken the savage chains,
fear has consumed what is to come: now they have filled the houses
and the temples, and the thankless altars are walled with lamentation.
One and the same terror comes upon all the years:
the old men ask for death, the youth burns and turns pale,
the halls tremble, wailed over with women's complaints,
the boys weep and cannot learn the causes of their weeping,
stunned and only trembling at their mothers' laments,
love drives the women, and the desperate have no shame:
they themselves hand weapons to the men, they themselves supply
wrath and courage, they exhort, and rush together, and groaning
cease not to show the ancestral thresholds and their little sons:
so when the shepherd, about to plunder from the pumice cave,
has roused the armed bees, the rough cloud roars,
and in turn they exhort one another with their hum, and all
fly at the enemy's face; soon, their wings failing,
they embrace their golden home and lament the captive
honey, and press the wrought wax to their breasts.
Nor does the divided will of the wavering crowd cease to fight
and sow discordant movements: these bid them give back the brother —
nor do they mutter it, but openly with voice and loud uproar —
to give back the kingdom; the reverence for the king has perished
in the anxious: 'Let him come and reckon here the bargained year,
and let the exile, unhappy, greet the Cadmean home
and his native darkness; but why should I atone with blood
for the frauds and the perjured crimes of a king's guilt?'
Then others: 'That loyalty is too late, now he prefers to conquer.'
Others beg Tiresias with tears and a suppliant throng,
and what is the one solace in their hard straits,
they ask to know the future; he holds shut and presses down
the fates of the gods: 'Was it not because our leader well trusted
my counsels and warnings before, when I forbade the faithless wars?
You, however, unhappy and doomed Thebe,' he says,
'if I keep silent, I cannot, wretched, hear you fall
and drink the Argive fire with my empty eyes,
let us be conquered, Piety; come, lay out the altars, maiden,
let us seek the gods.' She does it, and with keen gaze
the bloody points of the flames and the double fire upon the altar
and yet the clear summit of light arising in their midst
he points out; then in the empty shape of a serpent
he shows the redness rolled in a doubtful coil and broken,
faltering, and he lights up his father's darkness,
he has long since embraced the crowned fires,
drinking in the prophetic vapour with his burning face.
His hair stands grim with horror, and his frenzied locks
lift up the fillets that press them: you would think his torn-open
eyes and the brightness, long consumed, had returned to his cheeks.
At last he gave words to the overflowing frenzy:

title: Thebais
text:
'Hear, O guilty ones, the last offerings of the gods,
sons of Labdacus: kindly safety comes, but by a hard road.
The serpent of Mars demands funeral offerings and savage
rites: let whoever is last surviving of the viper's
brood fall; only by this bargain is victory given.
Happy is he who shall leave the light at so great a price.'
Near the savage altars of the prophetic seer there stood,
mournful, mourning as yet only the common fate
of his country, Creon: the great stroke of the sudden bolt,
no otherwise than if his breast were pierced by a hurled point,
lifeless he receives, and feels Menoeceus demanded.
For fear shows it and persuades; the anxious father is stunned,
his heart freezing with deep dread: as the Trinacrian shore
takes the sea recoiling from the Libyan tide,
soon he begs the seer, full of Phoebus and bidding him hasten,
now humbly clasping his knees, now begging the prophet
in vain to keep silent his lips as they chant; already rumour,
embracing the consecrated voice, flies, and Thebes cried the oracle aloud.
Now come, who gave the goads and the joys of a glorious death
to the youth — for never has this mind been transmitted to man
by absent gods — begin, mindful Clio,
since the ages and ordered antiquity are in your keeping.
A goddess, companion close beside the throne of Jove, from whom over the world
it is wont to be given rarely and to fall to earth, Virtue,
whether the almighty father grants her or she herself has chosen
to enter capacious men, how then she sprang down,
rejoicing, from the heavenly tracts! The bright stars give place
to her as she passes, and the fires she herself had fixed in the pole.
And now she presses upon the earth, her face not far from the sky;
but she chose to change her features, and becomes prophetic Manto,
that full faith might be given to the response; and her former
face she puts off by deception, the horror and the vigour
have gone from her eyes, a little grace and a gentler honour
remained, and laying aside the iron she put on
the prophets' insignia; her robes flow down, and with a fillet
her grim hair is bound — for it had been laurel — yet the harsh
face betrays the goddess, and her too-great stride; so the Lydian wife
laughed at Amphitryon's son, stripped of his bristling
hide, ruining the Sidonian garments on his shoulders
and tangling the distaff and breaking the timbrels with his hand.

title: Thebais
text:
But she found you not unsightly for the rites and worthy to be bidden
such things, Menoeceus, as you stood before the Dircaean tower;
the threshold of the vast gate thrown open,
you were laying the Danaans low, and beside you Mavortian Haemon.
But though you are kinsmen and brothers in all things,
you are the first: round about lifeless heaps are piled;
every weapon strikes home, no stroke is without slaughter —
not yet was the goddess at hand — neither mind nor right hand rests,
nor do the greedy arms stand idle; the very Sphinx,
the guardian of his helmet, seems to rage, and quickened by the sight of blood
the image leaps and the scattered bronze gleams:
when the goddess checked the hilt and the right hand of the fighter:
'Great-souled youth, than whom Mars would not have recognized any
more surely of the arms-bearing seed of Cadmus,
leave these humble battles, this is not the valour owed by you:
the stars call you, and you shall send your soul to heaven; conceive higher things;
long has your father reveled in this at the glad altars,
this the fires and the entrails will, this Apollo urges:
they ask the earthborn one for all the blood of the fatherland,
rumour sings the warnings, the Cadmean people rejoice,
sure of you; seize the gods in your mind, seize the noble fate.
Go, I pray, hasten, lest Haemon next forestall you.'
So she speaks, and with her great right hand stroked silently
the breast of him as he hesitated, and left herself within his heart,
no more swiftly does the cypress, breathed on by the rays of the bolt,
drink in the hostile flames at root and crown,
than the youth, possessed in his breast by the great power,
lifted up his senses and seized upon the love of death.
But when he marked the gait and bearing of the goddess turned away
and saw Manto suddenly grow from the earth into the clouds,
he was struck dumb. 'We follow, whoever of the gods you have summoned,
nor do we obey slowly,' he says; and now drawing back
he yet transfixed the Pylian Agreus, who pressed against the rampart,
his squires receive him spent; then the crowd, as he went,
acclaimed him, the author of peace and the saviour and the god,
rejoicing, and fills him with honourable fires,
and now in his haste, breathless with running, he holds his way to the walls
and rejoices to have escaped his wretched parents,
when his father — and both stood still, and the voice stuck in each,
and their cheeks fell, at last the father spoke first:
'What new chance has snatched you from the arms you had begun?
What worse than war do you prepare? Tell me, son, your suppliant,
why is your gaze grim? Why this fierce pallor on your face,
and why do your eyes not stay upon your father's face?
You have heard the response, it is plain. By you and yours,
son, I pray, and by my years, and by the breasts of your wretched mother,
do not trust the seer, do not, boy! Do the gods deign
to goad a profane old man, whose sight is empty
and his orbs put out, and his punishment most like to dread
Oedipus? What if by ambush and crafty fraud
the king is acting, to whom in our last fate your
nobility and your valour, famous before the leaders, are a fear?
Perhaps these are his words, which we think the gods';
he gives the warning! Do not give your rein to a hot mind,
give space and a slight delay; ill does impulse manage all things;
this, I pray, grant to your father as a gift.
So may your temples be marked with the white of ripe years,
and may you yourself be a father, and to this same fear,
spirited one, may you come: do not go on to bereave my house.
Do strangers' fathers, then, and alien pledges
touch you? If you have shame, first pity your own.
This is piety, this true honour; there is only glory
and windy renown and titles hidden in death.
Nor as a fearful father do I bend you: go, join the battles,
go against the Danaan lines and through the swords that meet you;
I do not hold you: only let me, wretched, wash your trembling
wounds and dry the welling blood with my tears,
and send you again and again to the savage wars,
this Thebes prefers.' So he held his neck and hands,
clinging; but neither tears nor words moved
the youth, vowed to the gods; nay, while they pointed it out,
with silent guile he comes upon his father and turns away his fear:
'You are deceived, alas, and know not your true fears, best of fathers,
no warnings stir me, nor the utterances of raving seers,
nor do empty things move me: let cunning Tiresias chant
those things to himself and his daughter; not if Apollo himself,
the shrines unbarred, should rave at me hand to hand,
but a grievous mishap of my dear brother carries me
of my own will to the city: Haemon groans to me, wounded
by an Inachian spear; scarcely could I bring him from the mid-dust of battle
between the two lines, with Argos now, now holding him —
but I delay; go, restore the doubtful, or to the crowd that bears him
say, let them obey and carry him gently; I will seek Aetion,
skilled to bind wounds and to call back the flight
of the last blood.' So speaking his unfinished words
he fled; in him, his breast plunged in black gloom,
his senses were confounded; his piety wavers uncertain
and his fears are at odds, the Fates impel him to believe.

title: Thebais
text:
Meanwhile turbulent Capaneus drives over the level field
the warlike bands coming from the broken gates,
now the wings of horsemen, now the wedges of footmen,
and the cars that trample down the dead of their drivers;
the same man with stones and frequent whirlwind loosens
the high towers, the same drives the squadrons and steams in blood,
now he scatters new wounds, hurling with the swift lead,
now whirls his javelin high with his outflung arm,
and there is no rooftop's height his spear does not reach,
bringing down a man and returning drenched with slaughter.
Now neither Oeneus' son nor Hippomedon, slain,
nor the seer does the Pelopean phalanx, nor the Arcadian, believe him to be:
nay, that the souls of the comrades have come together and all
stand in a single body, so wholly does he fill all things; no man's age,
no dress, no beauty moves him; he rages alike
against fighters and suppliants; no one withstands him,
none tries the changes of war: from afar they shudder at the arms
of the raging man, his terrible plumes, and the front of his helmet.
But dutiful Menoeceus, on a chosen part of the walls,
now sacred to behold and more august than his wont in face,
as if suddenly let down to earth from the heavenly height,
took his stand, his helmet removed, clearly to be known,
and looked down on the lines of men, and with a deep cry
turned the field and bade silence upon the war:
'Gods of arms, and you, Phoebus, who with so great a death
grant me to die, give joy to Thebes,
which I have bargained for and bought, lavish, with all my blood.
Bear back the war and dash against captured Lerna
its base remnants, and nursing their transfixed backs
may father Inachus turn away from his dishonoured sons.
But to the Tyrians give back temples, fields, homes, marriages, children,
by my death: if I, the welcome victim, have helped you,
if not with stunned ears did I receive the seer's
counsels and drank them down with Thebes not yet believing,
pay these things for me to the Amphionian dwellings,
and, I pray, by your prayers win over my deceived father.'
So he speaks, and with his flashing sword seizes his noble
soul, that long since disdained his limbs and grieved to be held,
and with a single wound he breaks the soul he sought,
then with his blood he sprinkles the towers and hallows the walls,
and over the midst of the lines, his sword not yet sheathed,
he cast himself and tried to fall upon the savage Achaeans.
But Piety and Virtue, embracing him, bore his body
gently to the earth; for his spirit long since
asks itself a place before Jove and the topmost peak among the stars.

title: Thebais
text:
And now within the walls, recovered with no toil,
they bear the hero, rejoicing: of its own will the venerated
band of Tantalus' kin had withdrawn; he comes in a long column
between the necks of the young men, and with glad acclaim by all
the people he is sung above Cadmus and Amphion,
as founder; some heap his limbs, loosed in death,
with garlands, some with the honour of spring,
and lay the adored body in its native place. Soon, his praises
ended, they take up the war again; here the father, tearful, his anger
conquered, groans aloud, and at last the mother is given power to weep:
'Was it as a lustral victim for savage Thebes, illustrious boy,
and a devoted head, that I, a worthless mother, reared you?
What crime did I contrive, to whom of the gods so hateful?
I did not, turned back to a monstrous union, make over
my pledges anew, nor as a mother bear deadly grandsons to a son.
What does it matter? Jocasta enjoys her sons and sees them
leaders and ruling: I give savage expiations to the war,
that in turn — does this please you, author of the bolt —
the Oedipodean brothers may exchange their diadems!
Why do I complain of gods or men? You, savage Menoeceus,
you above all have hastened to extinguish your wretched mother.
Whence this love of death? What sacred madness in your mind?
What conceptions, or what ill-omened pledges did I bring forth,
so unlike myself? Doubtless the serpent of Mars,
and the earth that flowered with the new arms of our forefathers —
hence these grim spirits and too much of Mars in your breast,
and nothing of your mother; of your own will and unbidden, slain,
you burst into the mournful Fates, though they were unwilling.
But I dreaded the Danaans and the weapons of Capaneus:
this, this was the hand and the iron to be feared, which, mad,
I gave you myself. Do you see how the sword has spent itself in your throat?
No Danaan would have driven the point deeper.'
The unhappy woman would have spoken still more, and filled all things
with her complaints: her companions and the handmaids lead her away,
loathing them, consoling, and hold her in her chamber; she sits, her cheeks
gouged with much nail; she heeds not the day, not the words
of those who pray, nor turns the gaze she has left fixed on the ground,
now bereft of voice, now of mind; so the fierce tigress,
her young snatched away, abandoned beneath a Scythian cave,
lies and licks the traces of the warm rock;
nowhere her wrath, the savagery and hunger of her raging
mouth has settled; the untroubled herds and flocks pass by:
she looks at them as she lies; for where, on what shall she feed her teats,
or whom, awaited, shall she crush with her huge prey?

title: Thebais
text:
Thus far arms, trumpets, iron, and wounds: but now
Capaneus must be raised hand to hand into the star-bearing heights.
No longer must I sing in the customary manner of the seers;
a greater madness must be sought from the Aonian groves:
dare it all with me, you goddesses! Whether that frenzy was sent
from the deep night, and the Stygian sisters, following Capaneus'
standards, snatched arms against Jove,
or whether his valour passed all measure, or his glory was headlong,
or whether a great death was given by the fates, or whether glad
beginnings of evil, and the kindly wraths of the gods toward mortals.
Now earthly things grow base to the man, and he wearies of the deep
slaughter, and at last, his missiles spent both of the Greeks
and his own, he looked back at the sky with a wearied
hand; soon he measures the lofty heights with a grim gaze,
the countless steps, the side closed in by twin beams of wood,
and carries himself an airy path, and, dreadful from afar,
brandishes a many-cleft oak with a blazing light;
his arms glow together and a fire is kindled on his shield.
